claims.text: Valence electron concentration governs the superconducting behavior of the high-entropy alloy.
The starting material is a solid-solution alloy containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
Systematic changes in alloy composition modify the valence electron concentration.
Local lattice distortions and chemical disorder act as structural mediators of superconducting behavior.
Valence electron concentration influences the density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level affect the superconducting transition temperature.
Alloys with a valence electron concentration around 4.5–5.5 will have higher superconducting transition temperatures than alloys with lower or higher valence electron concentrations.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloy remains a solid solution without secondary-phase precipitation.
The exact relationship between valence electron concentration and superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is unclear.
Lattice dynamics may also influence superconductivity in the alloy.
Electron-phonon coupling may also influence superconductivity in the alloy.
Failure to observe a correlation between valence electron concentration and superconducting transition temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
